items.question: What is the difference between a class instance and a struct instance after assignment?
items.answer: A class variable stores a reference to a heap object, so assignment copies the reference and both variables observe the same mutations. A struct assignment copies all fields; later changes to one copy do not affect the other. Interviewers often follow up with when copying is expensive and why cache keys and coordinates are usually `readonly struct`.
followUps: When does boxing a struct allocate?
Why is a mutable struct in a List a trap?
items.sixtySeconds: Class: shared identity via reference. Struct: independent copy. Use class for services and identity; small immutable data as readonly struct.

items.question: Explain get, set, init, and the C# 14 field keyword.
items.answer: `get` reads the value. `set` mutates after construction. `init` allows assignment only during object initialization (constructor or object initializer). The `field` keyword inside an accessor refers to a compiler-synthesized backing field, so you can validate in `set` without declaring `_msg` yourself. Name collisions with an existing member named `field` need `@field` or a rename.
followUps: How does init interact with records and with-expressions?
What breaking change can field cause in existing types?
items.sixtySeconds: init is construction-time set. field is the hidden store in the accessor. Keep fields private; properties are the API.

items.question: When do you use ref, in, and out instead of ordinary parameters?
items.answer: Ordinary parameters copy the value (or the reference for classes). `ref` aliases an existing variable both ways. `in` is a readonly alias — useful for large readonly structs to skip the copy. `out` is a definite-assignment contract: the callee must write it before returning. Do not reach for `ref` on every hot path; measure, and prefer `readonly struct` plus `in`.
followUps: Why can in still copy a mutable struct?
items.sixtySeconds: Ordinary first. ref = alias. in = readonly alias. out = must assign. Defensive copies bite mutable structs.

items.question: How do primary constructors and required properties change construction?
items.answer: Primary constructors (C# 12) put parameters on the type declaration and make them available in the body and field initializers. `required` properties (C# 11) force object initializers to set those members or the compiler errors. Together they replace telescoping constructor overloads for data-transfer types without hiding invalid empty objects.
followUps: Can a struct parameterless constructor differ from default(T)?
How do you validate primary-constructor parameters?
items.sixtySeconds: Primary ctor captures inputs on the type. required makes initializers complete. default(T) still zero-inits structs without running your ctor.

items.question: List C# access modifiers a senior should name, including file.
items.answer: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, private protected, and file for file-local types. Members default to private; top-level types default to internal. protected internal is union (assembly or derived). private protected is intersection (derived and same assembly). file is for source generators and collision-free helpers, not a member modifier on ordinary classes.
followUps: How is this different from TypeScript private?
When is internal seen by InternalsVisibleTo?
items.sixtySeconds: CLR enforces accessibility. file-local types never leak across files. protected internal vs private protected is a favorite trap.

items.question: Should you implement a finalizer on a class that wraps SkiaSharp?
items.answer: Almost never. Implement IDisposable (and IAsyncDisposable if needed) and use `using`. Finalizers are a garbage-collection topic (module 14) — they delay collection, run on a dedicated thread, and are easy to get wrong. Extension members that look like instance APIs are module 10, not a substitute for wrapping resources.
followUps: What is the Dispose pattern versus a finalizer?
Where do C# 14 extension members live in this curriculum?
items.sixtySeconds: Dispose with using. Finalizers: module 14. Extensions: module 10. Do not mix those answers.

items.question: What is a partial type and why do source generators use it?
items.answer: A partial type is one class, struct, or record split across multiple source files. Every part uses the `partial` keyword and the compiler merges them. Source generators emit one part (declarations, attributes, boilerplate) while you write another (business logic). C# 14 extended partial to constructors and events so generators can declare surfaces and you implement them.
followUps: How many primary constructors can a partial type have?
What is the difference between partial method and partial constructor?
items.sixtySeconds: partial = one type, many files. Generator declares, you implement. Only one primary constructor across all parts.

items.question: When should you overload operators on a custom type?
items.answer: Overload operators on value-like types with clear math semantics — money, coordinates, time ranges. Operators are public static methods with special syntax. Pair `==` with `Equals` and `GetHashCode`. C# 14 compound assignment (`+=`) lets mutable value types update in place. Do not overload operators on service classes or use implicit conversions that hide parsing failures.
followUps: What happens if you overload == but not GetHashCode?
How does C# 14 compound assignment differ from x = x + y?
items.sixtySeconds: Operators on value types only. == needs Equals/GetHashCode. C# 14 += avoids struct copy. No implicit string conversions.
